Both modules share the core infrastructure but differ in their parameter requirements and underlying PRODIGY library calls ([prodigyprotein.py](src/haddock/modules/scoring/prodigyprotein/prodigy.py#L1-L79), [prodigylig.py](src/haddock/modules/scoring/prodigyligand/prodigylig.py#L1-L86)).

## Installation and Verification

PRODIGY scoring requires external Python packages that are not part of the core HADDOCK3 installation. The `CheckInstall` class automatically validates the availability of these libraries at runtime ([libprodigy.py](src/haddock/libs/libprodigy.py#L20-L46)).

**Installation:**
```bash
pip install prodigy-prot prodigy-lig
```

> [!TIP]
> The installation verification occurs automatically when PRODIGY modules are executed. If the libraries are missing, HADDOCK3 raises a `ModuleError` with installation instructions, preventing silent failures.

## Parameter Reference

### PRODIGY Protein Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Range | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `chains` | list | `[]` | 0-20 items | Chain identifiers for scoring. Empty lists consider all inter-chain contacts. Groups can be specified with commas (e.g., `["A,B", "C"]` treats A and B as a single group interacting with C) |
| `distance_cutoff` | float | `5.5` | 1.0-100.0 Å | Distance cutoff for extracting amino acid contacts between chains |
| `accessibility_cutoff` | float | `0.05` | 0.0-1.0 | Solvent accessibility threshold for buried surface area analysis |
| `temperature` | float | `25.00` | -273.15-95.0°C | Temperature for pKd conversion from ΔG |
| `to_pkd` | boolean | `true` | - | Convert ΔG (kcal/mol) to pKd values |

**Chain Parameter Examples:**
- `[]` or `[A, B, C]` → Calculates contacts between all chain pairs
- `["A", "B"]` → Only A-B contacts considered
- `["A,B", "C"]` → A and B treated as single unit interacting with C

Sources: [defaults.yaml](src/haddock/modules/scoring/prodigyprotein/defaults.yaml#L1-L65)

### PRODIGY Ligand Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Range | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `receptor_chain` | string | `"A"` | 1 character | Chain ID of the receptor protein |
| `ligand_chain` | string | `"B"` | 1 character | Chain ID containing the ligand |
| `ligand_resname` | string | `"UNK"` | 1-3 characters | Residue name of the ligand in the PDB file |
| `electrostatics` | boolean | `true` | - | Use electrostatic component from HADDOCK model REMARKs |
| `distance_cutoff` | float | `10.5` | 1.0-100.0 Å | Distance cutoff for extracting receptor residues contacting the ligand |
| `temperature` | float | `25.00` | -273.15-95.0°C | Temperature for pKd conversion |
| `to_pkd` | boolean | `true` | - | Convert ΔG (kcal/mol) to pKd values |

Sources: [defaults.yaml](src/haddock/modules/scoring/prodigyligand/defaults.yaml#L1-L77)

## Scoring Pipeline Execution

The PRODIGY scoring workflow follows a consistent pattern regardless of the interaction type:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Input PDB Models] --> B[ProdigyJob Initialization]
    B --> C{Worker Selection}
    C -->|Protein-Protein| D[ProdigyProtein Worker]
    C -->|Protein-Ligand| E[ProdigyLigand Worker]
    
    D --> F[Parse Structure<br/>prodigy_prot.modules.parsers]
    E --> G[Parse Structure<br/>PDBParser/FastMMCIFParser]
    
    F --> H[Initialize PRODIGY<br/>with parameters]
    G --> I[Initialize ProdigyLig<br/>with receptor/ligand specs]
    
    H --> J[Predict Binding Affinity<br/>contact-based calculation]
    I --> K[Predict Binding Affinity<br/>with optional electrostatics]
    
    J --> L{Output Format}
    K --> L
    
    L -->|to_pkd=true| M[Convert ΔG to pKd<br/>using thermodynamic formula]
    L -->|to_pkd=false| N[Return ΔG kcal/mol]
    
    M --> O[ModelScore Object<br/>with rounded value]
    N --> O
    
    O --> P[Write to TSV file<br/>scoring.tsv]
    P --> Q[Next Module]
```

The execution pipeline demonstrates how both scoring variants converge on common post-processing steps while maintaining distinct evaluation logic appropriate to their molecular contexts.

### ΔG to pKd Conversion

When `to_pkd=true`, the system converts the PRODIGY-predicted ΔG (kcal/mol) to pKd using the thermodynamic relationship:

```python
ΔG_joules = ΔG × CALS_TO_JOULES × 1000
Kd = exp(-ΔG_joules / (R_GAS_CONST × kelvins))
pKd = -log10(Kd)
```

Where:
- `CALS_TO_JOULES = 4.184` (calories to joules conversion)
- `R_GAS_CONST = 8.31446261815324` J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹
- `kelvins = temperature + 273.15` (Celsius to Kelvin)

The temperature parameter is critical for accurate pKd conversion, as binding affinity is temperature-dependent.

Sources: [libprodigy.py](src/haddock/libs/libprodigy.py#L75-L128)

## Configuration Examples

### Protein-Protein Scoring

Basic configuration for evaluating protein-protein complexes:

```yaml
# Using defaults - all chains considered
prodigyprotein:
  to_pkd: true
  temperature: 25.00

# Antibody-antigen with chain grouping
prodigyprotein:
  chains: ["A,B", "C"]  # Heavy+Light chains as unit vs Antigen
  to_pkd: true
  temperature: 37.00  # Physiological temperature
  distance_cutoff: 5.5
  accessibility_cutoff: 0.05
```

Sources: [prodigy-protein-protein-test.cfg](examples/scoring/prodigy-protein-protein-test.cfg), [prodigy-antibody-antigen-test.cfg](examples/scoring/prodigy-antibody-antigen-test.cfg)

### Protein-Ligand Scoring

Configuration for protein-ligand complexes:

```yaml
prodigyligand:
  receptor_chain: "A"
  ligand_chain: "B"
  ligand_resname: "HEM"  # Adjust to your ligand name
  electrostatics: true    # Use HADDOCK electrostatics
  distance_cutoff: 10.5
  temperature: 25.00
  to_pkd: true
```

The `electrostatics` parameter leverages electrostatic calculations performed by HADDOCK during refinement stages, which are stored in the PDB file's REMARK section.

Sources: [prodigy-protein-ligand-test.cfg](examples/scoring/prodigy-protein-ligand-test.cfg)

### Integration in Complete Workflows

PRODIGY scoring is typically used as a post-refinement evaluation step:

```yaml
# Complete docking workflow with PRODIGY evaluation
topoaa:
  mode: local
rigidbody:
  sampling: 1000
refine:
  mode: all
mdref:
  mode: all
prodigyprotein:
  chains: []
  to_pkd: true
```

This pattern allows you to evaluate the quality of refined models using an independent, physics-informed scoring metric.

## Output Format

Both PRODIGY modules generate a `scoring.tsv` file containing one row per model with the following columns:

| Column | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `model` | Model filename or identifier |
| `score` | Predicted binding affinity (pKd or ΔG depending on `to_pkd` parameter) |

The scores are rounded to 3 decimal places for pKd and 3 decimal places for ΔG values, providing sufficient precision for ranking models without excessive significant digits.

Sources: [libprodigy.py](src/haddock/libs/libprodigy.py#L131-L137), [libprodigy.py](src/haddock/libs/libprodigy.py#L114-L128)

## Error Handling and Validation

The PRODIGY integration includes comprehensive error handling at multiple levels:

**Installation Level:** The `CheckInstall` class validates that `prodigy_prot` and `prodigy_lig` packages are available before attempting any scoring operations ([libprodigy.py](src/haddock/libs/libprodigy.py#L20-L46)).

**Execution Level:** Each worker wraps the PRODIGY library calls in try-catch blocks, capturing exceptions and storing them in the `ModelScore.error` field ([libprodigy.py](src/haddock/libs/libprodigy.py#L155-L163)). This allows the workflow to continue processing other models even if individual models fail.

**Logging Level:** PRODIGY's internal logging is suppressed at the CRITICAL level to prevent excessive output during batch processing ([libprodigy.py](src/haddock/libs/libprodigy.py#L61-L62)).

## Performance Considerations

PRODIGY scoring is computationally efficient compared to traditional scoring methods that require extensive energy calculations. Key performance characteristics:

- **Speed:** Typically < 1 second per model for both protein-protein and protein-ligand variants
- **Memory:** Low memory footprint as PRODIGY uses lightweight structural features
- **Scalability:** Suitable for evaluating hundreds to thousands of models in a single run
- **Parallelization:** The module can be combined with HADDOCK3's MPI parallelization for large-scale scoring jobs

## Integration with HADDOCK3 Workflow

The PRODIGY modules are fully integrated into the HADDOCK3 module system and can be combined with other analysis and scoring modules:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Sampling
        RB[Rigid Body]
    end
    
    subgraph Refinement
        EM[EM Scoring]
        MD[MD Refinement]
        MDS[MD Scoring]
    end
    
    subgraph Analysis
        FCC[FCC Clustering]
        CAPR[CAPRI Evaluation]
        PROD[PRODIGY Scoring]
    end
    
    RB --> EM --> MD --> MDS --> FCC --> CAPR
    MDS --> PROD
    CAPR --> PROD
    PROD --> Final[Final Model Selection]
```

> [!TIP]
> PRODIGY scoring is most valuable when used alongside traditional HADDOCK scoring and CAPRI evaluation. The combination provides complementary perspectives: physics-based energy calculations (HADDOCK), interface quality assessment (CAPRI), and binding affinity prediction (PRODIGY).

## Testing and Validation

Integration tests verify both module variants with various parameter combinations:

- **Default parameters:** Ensures baseline functionality with standard settings
- **Temperature variations:** Validates pKd conversion across different temperatures
- **Distance cutoff modifications:** Tests impact of contact definition changes
- **Accessibility adjustments:** Verifies BSA threshold functionality
- **Electrostatic components:** Tests optional electrostatic usage in ligand scoring

These tests use mock data representing real protein complexes and small molecules, ensuring the modules work correctly in production scenarios.

Sources: [test_prodigyprotein.py](integration_tests/test_prodigyprotein.py#L1-L132), [test_prodigyligand.py](integration_tests/test_prodigyligand.py#L1-L156)

## Best Practices

1. **Chain Selection:** For antibody-antigen complexes, explicitly group heavy and light chains using the `chains` parameter to treat the antibody as a single interacting unit

2. **Temperature Consistency:** Match the `temperature` parameter to your experimental conditions when comparing predicted affinities to measured binding data

3. **Electrostatics Usage:** Enable `electrostatics=true` for protein-ligand scoring only when your models have undergone refinement with electrostatic calculations in HADDOCK

4. **Combined Scoring:** Use PRODIGY scores in conjunction with HADDOCK scores and clustering metrics for comprehensive model evaluation

5. **Output Format:** Consider using `to_pkd=false` if you prefer working with ΔG values directly, especially when comparing to thermodynamic measurements

## Next Steps

- To understand how PRODIGY scoring fits into the broader HADDOCK3 evaluation framework, see [HADDOCK Scoring Function Components](19-haddock-scoring-function-components)
- For comprehensive result analysis workflows, explore [Result Analysis and Interpretation](25-result-analysis-and-interpretation)
- To learn about other specialized scoring methods like EM-based scoring, refer to [Energy Minimization vs MD Scoring](20-energy-minimization-vs-md-scoring)
- For complete workflow design including PRODIGY evaluation, consult [Custom Workflow Design](27-custom-workflow-design)

# Clustering Algorithms (FCC and RMSD)



HADDOCK3 provides two complementary clustering approaches to organize and analyze docking results: **Fraction of Common Contacts (FCC)** clustering and **RMSD-based clustering**. These algorithms enable you to group structurally similar models, identify representative solutions, and reduce computational complexity in subsequent refinement stages. Understanding when and how to apply each method is crucial for effective docking workflow design.

## Overview of Clustering in HADDOCK3

Clustering serves as a critical post-processing step in HADDOCK3 workflows, serving three primary purposes: reducing redundant solutions, identifying consensus binding modes, and selecting representative models for further refinement. The choice between FCC and RMSD clustering depends on your specific scientific objectives, the type of molecular interaction, and the characteristics of your sampling results.

HADDOCK3's clustering architecture integrates with the broader workflow through modular design, enabling seamless execution after sampling modules like `rigidbody` or `flexref`. Both clustering approaches output standardized files containing cluster assignments, ranked cluster lists, and model-level annotations that propagate through subsequent workflow stages.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Input
        A[Models from Sampling]
    end
    
    subgraph FCC_Path
        B1[Calculate Contacts<br/>contact_fcc executable]
        B2[Compute FCC Matrix<br/>calculate_pairwise_matrix]
        B3[Taylor-Butina Clustering<br/>Asymmetric algorithm]
        B4[FCC Clusters Output]
    end
    
    subgraph RMSD_Path
        C1[Load RMSD Matrix<br/>from rmsdmatrix module]
        C2[Hierarchical Clustering<br/>scipy linkage]
        C3[Cut Dendrogram<br/>distance or maxclust]
        C4[RMSD Clusters Output]
    end
    
    subgraph Common_Output
        D[cluster.out]
        E[clust*.tsv]
        F[clust*.txt]
        G[HTML Matrix Visualization]
    end
    
    A --> B1 --> B2 --> B3 --> B4
    A --> C1 --> C2 --> C3 --> C4
    B4 --> D
    C4 --> D
    B4 --> E
    C4 --> E
    B4 --> F
    C4 --> F
    B4 --> G
    C4 --> G
```

Sources: [src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustfcc/__init__.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustfcc/__init__.py), [src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustrmsd/__init__.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustrmsd/__init__.py)

## FCC Clustering: Fraction of Common Contacts

**FCC clustering** groups models based on similarity of their intermolecular contact patterns rather than geometric superposition. This approach is particularly valuable for protein-protein, protein-peptide, and protein-DNA interactions where the binding interface topology is more informative than global structural alignment. The method was originally described by Rodrigues et al. (2012) and has been implemented in HADDOCK3 with algorithmic optimizations for large-scale analysis.

### Core Algorithm Implementation

The FCC clustering workflow follows a three-stage pipeline. First, the `contact_fcc` executable identifies atomic contacts within a user-defined distance cutoff (default 5.0Å). This C++ implementation processes PDB files efficiently, handling chain segmentation and residue identification while ignoring hydrogens and HETATM records [src/haddock/deps/contact_fcc.cpp](src/haddock/deps/contact_fcc.cpp#L23-L35). Contact residues are encoded as unique integers incorporating chain and residue information, enabling fast set operations for similarity calculations.

The second stage computes a pairwise FCC matrix where each entry represents the fraction of common contacts between two models. The calculation uses asymmetric FCC values (FCC_AB and FCC_BA) to account for differences in interface sizes, implementing strictness factors to prevent small interfaces from clustering promiscuously with larger ones [src/haddock/libs/libfcc.py](src/haddock/libs/libfcc.py#L140-L148). The strictness parameter (default 0.75) multiplies the clustering cutoff for the second direction, allowing controlled variability while maintaining biological relevance.

The final stage applies the **Asymmetric Taylor-Butina Disjoint Clustering Algorithm**, a greedy iterative method that selects cluster centers based on neighbor count and progressively assigns unclustered models to the most appropriate cluster [src/haddock/fcc/cluster_fcc.py](src/haddock/fcc/cluster_fcc.py#L69-L96). This approach ensures each model belongs to exactly one cluster and prioritizes large, well-populated clusters over smaller singletons.

### Key Classes and Data Structures

FCC clustering centers on two fundamental classes defined in the library module. The `Element` class represents individual models with attributes for name, cluster assignment, and neighbor relationships [src/haddock/libs/libfcc.py](src/haddock/libs/libfcc.py#L7-L24). Each Element maintains a set of neighboring Elements that satisfy the FCC similarity criteria, enabling efficient cluster formation.

The `Cluster` class encapsulates clustering results with a name, center Element, and member list [src/haddock/libs/libfcc.py](src/haddock/libs/libfcc.py#L26-L66). The `populate()` method automatically assigns all unclustered neighbors of the center to the cluster, while the `add_member()` method allows manual addition of specific models. Cluster size calculations include both center and members, providing accurate population statistics for ranking.

### Configuration Parameters

FCC clustering exposes five key configuration parameters in `defaults.yaml`:

| Parameter | Type | Default | Range | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `contact_distance_cutoff` | float | 5.00 | 2.00-999.99 | Maximum distance (Å) for atomic contact detection. Smaller values increase specificity but may miss relevant contacts. |
| `clust_cutoff` | float | 0.60 | 0.00-1.00 | Minimum FCC value for models to belong to same cluster. Higher values produce stricter clustering. |
| `min_population` | integer | 4 | 1-9999 | Minimum cluster size threshold. Clusters with fewer members are discarded. The algorithm iteratively reduces this value if no clusters are found. |
| `strictness` | float | 0.75 | 0.00-1.00 | Multiplier for asymmetric FCC calculation. Lower values increase clustering promiscuity for small interfaces. |
| `plot_matrix` | boolean | false | - | Enable generation of HTML matrix visualization for interactive cluster inspection. |

Sources: [src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustfcc/defaults.yaml](src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustfcc/defaults.yaml)

### Practical Considerations

FCC clustering excels in scenarios where interface conservation is more important than global structural alignment. For antibody-antigen complexes, the method groups solutions sharing similar paratope-epitope contact patterns, even when overall orientations differ. Similarly, for protein-DNA docking, FCC clusters models with analogous contact footprints on the nucleic acid surface, facilitating identification of conserved binding modes [docs/examples.md](docs/examples.md#docking-protein-dna).

> [!TIP]
> The `strictness` parameter requires careful tuning based on your system's interface characteristics. For small peptides binding to large protein surfaces, increase strictness (0.85-0.95) to prevent clustering of spurious contacts. For protein-protein interactions with large, well-defined interfaces, default or lower strictness (0.65-0.75) provides reasonable sensitivity.

FCC clustering requires contact calculation for all input models, which can be computationally expensive for large ensembles (>10,000 models). However, the resulting clusters tend to be more biologically interpretable since they reflect interface conservation rather than global structural similarity. The method is particularly robust to conformational changes away from the binding interface.

## RMSD Clustering: Hierarchical Geometric Grouping

**RMSD clustering** organizes models based on geometric similarity using hierarchical clustering on pre-computed RMSD matrices. This traditional approach groups structures with similar overall orientations, making it ideal for systems where global binding pose is the primary distinguishing feature, such as protein-ligand docking or symmetric complex assembly.

### Integration with RMSD Matrix Module

RMSD clustering depends on the `rmsdmatrix` module to generate the pairwise distance matrix. The RMSD matrix module calculates all-atom or interface-ligand RMSD values using an optimized C implementation, with options to restrict calculations to specific residues via the `resdic_` parameter [src/haddock/modules/analysis/rmsdmatrix/__init__.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/rmsdmatrix/__init__.py#L16-L46). The matrix is stored in condensed format and passed between modules via the `rmsd_matrix.json` file, enabling multiple `clustrmsd` executions with different parameters on the same matrix.

### Hierarchical Clustering with SciPy

The `clustrmsd` module leverages scipy's hierarchical clustering implementation, supporting seven linkage methods for dendrogram construction:

| Linkage Method | Description | Use Case |
|----------------|-------------|----------|
| `average` | Average distance between all pairs of clusters | Default choice; balances single and complete linkage |
| `complete` | Maximum distance between cluster members | Produces compact, spherical clusters |
| `single` | Minimum distance between cluster members | Sensitive to noise; produces chaining effects |
| `ward` | Minimizes variance increase | Good for equally sized, compact clusters |
| `centroid` | Distance between cluster centroids | Can produce inversions in dendrogram |
| `median` | Weighted centroid distance | Less common; similar to centroid |
| `weighted` | Weighted average distance | Suitable for imbalanced cluster sizes |

Sources: [src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustrmsd/defaults.yaml](src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustrmsd/defaults.yaml#L16-L25)

The dendrogram construction follows the standard hierarchical clustering procedure, where models are iteratively merged based on pairwise RMSD distances until a single cluster remains [src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustrmsd/clustrmsd.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustrmsd/clustrmsd.py#L82-L88). The resulting linkage matrix is saved to `dendrogram.txt` for inspection and visualization purposes.

### Dendrogram Cutting Strategies

Two complementary strategies determine how the dendrogram is cut to produce final clusters. The `distance` criterion cuts the dendrogram at a specified RMSD threshold (`clust_cutoff`), grouping all models within that distance [src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustrmsd/clustrmsd.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustrmsd/clustrmsd.py#L90-L96). This approach produces clusters of varying sizes depending on the structural diversity of the input ensemble.

The `maxclust` criterion specifies the desired number of clusters (`n_clusters`), cutting the dendrogram to produce exactly that many groups [src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustrmsd/clustrmsd.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustrmsd/clustrmsd.py#L90-L96). This strategy is useful when you want to control the number of representative models for downstream processing, though cluster quality depends on the inherent structure of the data.

> [!TIP]
> When using the `distance` criterion, apply the `min_population` filter iteratively rather than as a strict cutoff. The `iterate_min_population` function progressively relaxes the population threshold if no clusters satisfy the requirement, ensuring you obtain meaningful clusters even from challenging datasets.

### Cluster Center Identification

RMSD clustering identifies representative structures by computing the model with minimum average RMSD to all other cluster members [src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustrmsd/clustrmsd.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustrmsd/clustrmsd.py#L35-L67). This "medoid" selection ensures the center is a actual model from the ensemble rather than a theoretical average, maintaining structural validity for subsequent refinement stages.

### Configuration Parameters

RMSD clustering provides six configuration parameters:

| Parameter | Type | Default | Range | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------|-------------|
| `linkage` | string | average | - | Method for hierarchical clustering. Affects dendrogram structure. |
| `criterion` | string | distance | distance/maxclust | Strategy for cutting dendrogram. |
| `clust_cutoff` | float | 7.5 | 0.1-100 | RMSD threshold (Å) when criterion=`distance`. Higher values produce fewer, larger clusters. |
| `min_population` | integer | 4 | 1-9999 | Minimum cluster size. Ignored when criterion=`maxclust`. |
| `n_clusters` | integer | 4 | 1-9999 | Desired number of clusters when criterion=`maxclust`. Ignored otherwise. |
| `plot_matrix` | boolean | false | - | Enable HTML matrix visualization with color-coded RMSD values. |

Sources: [src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustrmsd/defaults.yaml](src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustrmsd/defaults.yaml)

### Practical Considerations

RMSD clustering is particularly effective for protein-ligand docking where global binding orientation distinguishes meaningful solutions. The method groups ligands with similar binding poses, enabling identification of consensus binding modes even when the ligand undergoes conformational rearrangement [docs/examples.md](docs/examples.md#docking-protein-ligand).

For glycan-protein interactions, RMSD clustering can be complemented with interface-ligand RMSD (ilRMSD) calculations through the `ilrmsdmatrix` module, focusing similarity assessment on the glycan's binding pose rather than overall protein orientation [docs/examples.md](docs/examples.md#docking-protein-glycan). This hybrid approach captures both global binding mode and interface-specific conservation.

## Common Clustering Infrastructure

Both clustering algorithms share substantial infrastructure through the `libclust` library, including cluster ranking, output formatting, and visualization generation. This common architecture ensures consistent user experience and facilitates switching between methods based on workflow requirements.

### Cluster Ranking and Scoring

Clusters are ranked by the average HADDOCK score of their top members, prioritizing energetically favorable solutions [src/haddock/libs/libclust.py](src/haddock/libs/libclust.py#L227-L260). The `rank_clusters()` function sorts cluster members by score, calculates the mean of the top `min_population` models, and returns a sorted list of clusters from best to worst. This scoring strategy identifies clusters with strong energetic signals rather than simply the most populated ones.

The ranking integrates with the model metadata through the `add_cluster_info()` function, which annotates each model with its cluster ID and rank assignment [src/haddock/libs/libclust.py](src/haddock/libs/libclust.py#L260-L292). These annotations propagate through subsequent workflow stages, enabling downstream modules to make cluster-aware decisions during model selection.

### Output File Generation

Both clustering modules generate three primary output files with standardized formats. The `cluster.out` file contains simple cluster listings with center and member indices, providing compatibility with legacy HADDOCK analysis tools [src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustfcc/clustfcc.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustfcc/clustfcc.py#L42-L62). The `.tsv` files (e.g., `clustfcc.tsv`, `clustrmsd.tsv`) provide tab-separated model listings with cluster assignments, scores, and rankings for programmatic access.

The detailed cluster reports (`clustfcc.txt`, `clustrmsd.txt`) contain comprehensive information including clustering parameters, cluster statistics (size, mean score, standard deviation), and member lists with score annotations [src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustfcc/clustfcc.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustfcc/clustfcc.py#L105-L210). Cluster centers are marked with asterisks for easy identification. These reports are ideal for publication-quality documentation and detailed analysis.

### Matrix Visualization

When `plot_matrix=true`, both modules generate interactive HTML visualizations of their respective similarity matrices [src/haddock/libs/libclust.py](src/haddock/libs/libclust.py#L62-L174). The FCC matrix displays contact-based similarities with color gradients (blue = similar), while the RMSD matrix uses reverse coloring (blue = distant). Cluster boundaries are delineated with white lines, and hover effects reveal exact pairwise values.

The visualization function handles large matrices efficiently, limiting display to 3100 entries (approximately 56 models) to prevent browser performance issues [src/haddock/libs/libclust.py](src/haddock/libs/libclust.py#L23). For larger ensembles, consider sub-sampling representative models or analyzing cluster-specific subsets.

## Algorithm Selection Guide

Choosing between FCC and RMSD clustering depends on your scientific objectives and system characteristics. Consider the following decision framework:

**Choose FCC clustering when:**
- Interface conservation is more informative than global orientation
- Working with protein-protein or protein-nucleic acid interactions
- Binding interfaces are well-defined and structurally conserved
- You want to group solutions with similar contact patterns regardless of overall pose
- Analyzing antibody-antigen or peptide-protein interactions with multiple binding modes

**Choose RMSD clustering when:**
- Global binding orientation is the primary distinguishing feature
- Working with protein-ligand or small molecule docking
- Systems exhibit large conformational changes away from binding interface
- You need to identify structurally similar binding poses
- Analyzing symmetric complexes or multi-component assemblies

**Consider hybrid approaches when:**
- Both interface and global orientation provide complementary information
- Systems exhibit intermediate characteristics (e.g., protein-glycan interactions)
- You want to compare clustering results from different perspectives

| Scenario | Recommended Method | Rationale |
|----------|-------------------|-----------|
| Protein-protein with NMR restraints | FCC | Interface restraints produce similar contact patterns |
| Protein-ligand with known binding site | RMSD | Global orientation distinguishes binding modes |
| Antibody-antigen with multiple epitopes | FCC | Contact patterns identify epitope-specific solutions |
| Protein-DNA with sequence-specific binding | FCC | Base-specific contacts cluster effectively |
| Symmetric homotrimer assembly | RMSD | Global symmetry constraints produce structural groups |
| Protein-glycan with flexible sugar | ilRMSD/RMSD | Hybrid captures local glycan pose and global binding |

## Workflow Integration Examples

### Example 1: Standard Protein-Protein Docking

```yaml
modules:
  - rigidbody:
      sampling: 1000
  - caprieval:
      reference: ./data/reference.pdb
  - clustfcc:
      clust_cutoff: 0.60
      min_population: 4
  - seletopclusts:
      top_cluster: 10
      top_model: 10
  - flexref:
  - emref:
```

This workflow generates 1000 rigid-body models, applies FCC clustering to group interface-similar solutions, selects the top 10 models from each of the best 10 clusters, and performs flexible refinement. The FCC clustering ensures diverse interface chemistries are represented in downstream refinement.

### Example 2: Protein-Ligand with RMSD Clustering

```yaml
modules:
  - rigidbody:
      sampling: 1000
  - rmsdmatrix:
      resdic_: [1-100]  # Focus on protein binding site
  - clustrmsd:
      linkage: average
      criterion: distance
      clust_cutoff: 5.0
      min_population: 2
  - seletopclusts:
      top_cluster: 5
      top_model: 5
  - emref:
```

This protein-ligand workflow uses RMSD clustering restricted to the binding site via `resdic_`, grouping ligands with similar binding orientations regardless of minor conformational differences. The relatively loose cutoff (5.0Å) accommodates ligand flexibility while distinguishing major binding modes.

### Example 3: Multiple Clustering Strategies

```yaml
modules:
  - rigidbody:
      sampling: 2000
  - clustfcc:
      contact_distance_cutoff: 5.0
      clust_cutoff: 0.65
      min_population: 4
  - clustrmsd:
      linkage: complete
      criterion: maxclust
      n_clusters: 20
```

This parallel clustering approach applies both FCC and RMSD clustering to the same sampling output, enabling comparison of interface-based and geometry-based grouping strategies. The FCC clustering produces biologically meaningful interface clusters, while RMSD clustering provides complementary structural groupings.

Sources: [docs/examples.md](docs/examples.md#general-analysis-tasks)

## Advanced Configuration and Troubleshooting

### Adjusting Clustering Stringency

The sensitivity of both clustering methods can be tuned through primary cutoff parameters. For FCC, reduce `clust_cutoff` (e.g., 0.50) to increase cluster size and sensitivity, or increase it (e.g., 0.75) for stricter grouping [src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustfcc/defaults.yaml](src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustfcc/defaults.yaml#L15-L24). The `strictness` parameter provides additional control over asymmetric relationships.

For RMSD clustering, `clust_cutoff` directly controls the distance threshold [src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustrmsd/defaults.yaml](src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustrmsd/defaults.yaml#L30-L36). Typical values range from 2.0Å (very strict) to 10.0Å (very loose), depending on system flexibility and desired granularity. The `linkage` method also affects cluster characteristics; `complete` linkage produces tighter clusters than `average`.

### Handling Challenging Datasets

When no clusters satisfy the `min_population` threshold, both algorithms implement adaptive strategies. The FCC module iteratively reduces `min_population` until at least one cluster is found [src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustfcc/clustfcc.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustfcc/clustfcc.py#L17-L38). The RMSD module provides the `iterate_min_population()` function for similar behavior when `criterion=distance` [src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustrmsd/clustrmsd.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustrmsd/clustrmsd.py#L120-L150).

If your dataset produces many singletons or very small clusters, consider: (1) relaxing similarity thresholds, (2) reducing `min_population`, (3) checking if contact cutoff is too restrictive (FCC), or (4) verifying RMSD calculation parameters (RMSD). Poor clustering often indicates insufficient sampling diversity or inappropriate parameter choices for your system.

### Performance Considerations

FCC clustering complexity scales as O(n²) for pairwise contact comparison plus O(n) for the greedy clustering algorithm. The contact calculation phase dominates runtime for large ensembles, with the C++ `contact_fcc` executable providing optimized performance. Parallel execution distributes contact calculations across available cores via the Job dispatcher [src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustfcc/__init__.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/clustfcc/__init__.py#L38-L50).

RMSD clustering efficiency depends on the pre-computed RMSD matrix. The `rmsdmatrix` module provides optimized C implementation with parallel support, handling up to 10,000 models by default [src/haddock/modules/analysis/rmsdmatrix/__init__.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/rmsdmatrix/__init__.py#L108-L115). The hierarchical clustering step in `clustrmsd` is O(n²) but typically fast for datasets under 5000 models.

For very large ensembles (>5000 models), consider pre-filtering with energy-based selection or initial coarse clustering before detailed analysis. The `seletop` module can reduce input size while preserving diversity based on score distributions.

## Next Steps

Now that you understand the clustering algorithms available in HADDOCK3, you can explore related analysis and visualization tools:

- [Contact Map Visualization](23-contact-map-visualization) - Visualize interfacial contacts within clusters
- [Alanine Scanning for Interface Analysis](24-alanine-scanning-for-interface-analysis) - Identify hotspot residues in clustered solutions
- [Result Analysis and Interpretation](25-result-analysis-and-interpretation) - Strategies for selecting final models from clustered ensembles

For practical implementation details, review the example workflows demonstrating clustering integration in [Usage Documentation](2-quick-start) and the analysis examples in `examples/analysis/` [docs/examples.md](docs/examples.md#general-analysis-tasks).

# Contact Map Visualization



The contactmap module provides comprehensive visualization and analysis of intermolecular contacts in protein complexes. This module generates interactive heatmaps and chord charts that reveal residue-residue interaction patterns across both individual structures and clustered docking results. By quantifying contact probabilities and distances, you can identify stable interaction interfaces, analyze binding modes, and extract mechanistic insights from your docking experiments.

## Architecture Overview

The contactmap module operates on two distinct analysis modes depending on whether input structures are clustered. The architecture comprises two primary analysis classes: `ContactsMap` for single-structure analysis and `ClusteredContactMap` for ensemble-based analysis of clustered models. Both classes implement a common `SupportsRun` interface, enabling flexible execution through HADDOCK3's scheduling system.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Input Models] --> B{Are Models Clustered?}
    B -->|No| C[ContactsMap Analysis]
    B -->|Yes| D[ClusteredContactMap Analysis]
    
    C --> E[Extract PDB Data]
    D --> F[Aggregate Cluster Data]
    
    E --> G[Compute Distance Matrix]
    F --> G
    
    G --> H[Generate Contact Data]
    H --> I{Output Types}
    
    I --> J[TSV Contact Files]
    I --> K[Interactive Heatmaps]
    I --> L[Chord Charts]
    I --> M[HTML Report]
    
    J --> N[Downstream Analysis]
    K --> N
    L --> N
    M --> N
```

The module integrates seamlessly with HADDOCK3's workflow engine, accepting `PDBFile` objects from previous steps and forwarding them unchanged to subsequent modules. This design pattern allows contact map analysis to be inserted at any point in the workflow without disrupting the model pipeline.

Sources: [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/__init__.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/__init__.py#L1-L14), [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py#L1-L5), [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py#L158-L294)

## Core Analysis Concepts

The contactmap module quantifies molecular interactions through two complementary metrics: Cα-Cα distances and shortest heavy-atom distances. Cα-Cα distances capture overall residue proximity and are particularly useful for identifying backbone-level interaction patterns, with a default threshold of 9.0 Å. The shortest heavy-atom distance metric provides atomic-level resolution by finding the minimum distance between any heavy atoms of two residues, using a more stringent default threshold of 4.5 Å.

For clustered analysis, the module aggregates contact data across all structures within a cluster. This aggregation enables computation of contact probabilities—the fraction of structures in a cluster where two residues satisfy the contact threshold. This probabilistic approach distinguishes consistent interface contacts from transient or artifact interactions, providing crucial insights into binding specificity.

> [!TIP]
> Contact probabilities in clustered analysis are normalized by cluster size, enabling direct comparison between clusters of different cardinalities. Use the `cluster_heatmap_datatype` parameter to switch between average distances and contact probabilities depending on your analytical needs.

The module also classifies residue-residue interactions by polarity type (polar-apolar, polar-polar, apolar-apolar, etc.), which is used in chord charts to color-code interaction ribbons according to chemical character. This classification follows standard biochemical categorization of amino acid properties.

Sources: [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py#L38-L75), [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/defaults.yaml](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/defaults.yaml#L1-L21), [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py#L292-L380)

## Configuration Parameters

The contactmap module offers extensive configurability through its parameter system. Understanding these parameters enables fine-tuning of analysis sensitivity and output presentation.

| Parameter | Type | Default | Range/Choices | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|--------------|-------------|
| `ca_ca_dist_threshold` | float | 9.0 | 4.0-1000.0 | Cα-Cα distance (Å) defining a contact |
| `shortest_dist_threshold` | float | 4.5 | 2.0-1000.0 | Minimum heavy-atom distance defining a contact |
| `color_ramp` | string | 'Greys' | Custom colorscales | Color scheme for heatmap visualization |
| `single_model_analysis` | boolean | false | - | Enable analysis for individual unclustered models |
| `generate_heatmap` | boolean | true | - | Generate interactive heatmap visualizations |
| `generate_chordchart` | boolean | true | - | Generate chord chart visualizations |
| `topX` | integer | 10 | 1-100 | Number of top unclustered models to analyze |
| `cluster_heatmap_datatype` | string | 'shortest-cont-probability' | See below | Data type for cluster heatmaps |
| `chordchart_datatype` | string | 'shortest-dist' | See below | Data type for chord charts |

The `cluster_heatmap_datatype` parameter supports four data representations:
- `ca-ca-dist`: Average Cα-Cα distances across the cluster
- `ca-ca-cont-probability`: Probability of Cα-Cα contact satisfaction
- `shortest-dist`: Average shortest heavy-atom distances
- `shortest-cont-probability`: Probability of heavy-atom contact satisfaction

For chord charts, which focus solely on intermolecular contacts, only distance-based options (`ca-ca-dist` and `shortest-dist`) are available as the visualization directly encodes distances in ribbon thickness.

Sources: [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/defaults.yaml](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/defaults.yaml#L1-L121), [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/__init__.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/__init__.py#L58-L124)

## Visualization Types

### Heatmap Visualization

Heatmaps provide a comprehensive matrix view of all residue-residue contacts, including both intra- and intermolecular interactions. The x- and y-axes represent individual residues ordered by chain and sequence position, while cell colors encode the chosen metric (distance or contact probability). This format enables rapid identification of interaction hotspots and comparative analysis across different clusters.

The module generates interactive Plotly heatmaps saved as HTML files, supporting zooming, hovering for detailed information, and color scale adjustments. The heatmaps utilize half-matrix representation (upper triangle only) to avoid redundancy, with diagonal elements representing each residue's self-contact.

> [!TIP]
> For large complexes, consider using a reversed colorscale (e.g., 'Greys_r') where darker colors represent shorter distances or higher contact probabilities. This matches intuitive expectations where stronger interactions are more visually prominent.

Heatmap generation leverages the `heatmap_plotly` function from `libplots.py`, which supports delineation traces for visual separation of chains and customizable hover templates for detailed interaction inspection.

Sources: [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py#L1071-L1195), [src/haddock/libs/libplots.py](src/haddock/libs/libplots.py#L1280-L1373)

### Chord Chart Visualization

Chord charts offer an intuitive circular representation focusing exclusively on intermolecular contacts. Residues are arranged as arcs around a circle, grouped by chain, with connecting ribbons representing contacts. Ribbon thickness encodes contact strength (inverse of distance), while ribbon colors reflect the chemical polarity of the interacting residue pair.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph DataPrep["Data Preparation"]
        A[Contact Matrix] --> B[Contact to Binary]
        C[Distance Matrix] --> D[Normalize for Thickness]
        E[Intertype Matrix] --> F[Assign Colors]
    end
    
    subgraph Visualization["Visualization Components"]
        G[Ideograms<br/>Residue Arcs]
        H[Ribbons<br/>Contact Connections]
        I[Legend<br/>Interaction Types]
    end
    
    DataPrep --> Visualization
    
    subgraph Layout["Plotly Layout"]
        J[Polar Coordinates]
        K[Interactive Controls]
        L[Hover Information]
    end
    
    Visualization --> Layout
```

The chord chart implementation employs sophisticated geometric calculations using Bézier curves to create smooth ribbon arcs connecting interacting residues. Each chain occupies a proportional segment of the circle, with gaps between chains for visual clarity. The `make_chordchart` function orchestrates this process, handling matrix transformations, ideogram arc generation, and ribbon construction.

Chord charts excel at revealing interface architecture and identifying key residue pairs that mediate intermolecular binding. The circular layout naturally highlights chain boundaries and enables rapid assessment of interface continuity.

Sources: [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py#L1902-L2151), [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py#L2253-L2378)

## Data Processing Pipeline

The contactmap module implements a systematic data processing pipeline that transforms raw PDB coordinates into structured contact information.

### Single Model Analysis

For individual structures, `ContactsMap` executes the following workflow:

1. **PDB Parsing**: Extract ATOM/HETATM records organized by chain and residue, maintaining chain order and residue sequence positions. The `extract_pdb_dt` function builds a hierarchical dictionary structure mapping chain → residue → atom data.

2. **Coordinate Extraction**: The `get_ordered_coords` function extracts atomic coordinates (default: Cα atoms only) and generates ordered residue keys in the format `chainid_resid`. This ordering ensures consistent matrix indexing.

3. **Distance Matrix Computation**: Using SciPy's `pdist` and `squareform` functions, compute an all-vs-all distance matrix between all extracted atoms. This N×N matrix serves as the foundation for all subsequent contact analysis.

4. **Contact Enumeration**: Iterate over all residue pairs (upper triangle only) to extract:
   - Cα-Cα distances
   - Shortest heavy-atom distances
   - Interaction polarity types
   - Chain identities for intermolecular filtering

5. **Output Generation**: Write contact data to TSV files and generate requested visualizations.

### Clustered Analysis

`ClusteredContactMap` extends single-model analysis through aggregation:

1. **Individual Processing**: For each model in the cluster, instantiate `ContactsMap` and extract contact data using the same pipeline as single-model analysis.

2. **Contact Aggregation**: The `aggregate_contacts` static method accumulates contact values across all cluster members. Each unique residue pair maintains lists of distances from all structures, enabling computation of averages and contact probabilities.

3. **Statistical Summarization**: Compute mean distances and contact probabilities by calculating the fraction of structures where each contact satisfies the defined threshold.

4. **Consolidated Output**: Generate aggregated TSV files and visualizations representing the cluster's consensus interaction pattern.

This aggregated approach robustly identifies persistent interface features while filtering out model-specific noise.

Sources: [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py#L652-L792), [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py#L172-L215), [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py#L307-L380)

## Output Structure

The contactmap module generates a hierarchical output structure organized by analysis type and target (single model or cluster).

### File Organization

```
contactmap_output/
├── ContactMapReport.html           # Master navigation page
├── cluster1/                       # Cluster-based analyses
│   ├── cluster1_contacts.tsv      # Aggregated contact data
│   ├── cluster1_contacts.html     # Interactive heatmap
│   └── cluster1_chordchart.html   # Interactive chord chart
├── cluster2/
│   └── [same structure as cluster1]
└── Unclustered_*/                  # Single model analyses (if enabled)
    ├── Unclustered_model1_contacts.tsv
    ├── Unclustered_model1_contacts.html
    └── Unclustered_model1_chordchart.html
```

### TSV File Format

The generated TSV files contain tab-separated contact data with the following columns:

| Column | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `res1` | First residue identifier (format: `chainid_resid_resname`) |
| `res2` | Second residue identifier |
| `ca-ca-dist` | Cα-Cα distance (Å) |
| `ca-ca-cont-probability` | Probability of Cα-Cα contact satisfaction |
| `shortest-dist` | Shortest heavy-atom distance (Å) |
| `shortest-cont-probability` | Probability of heavy-atom contact satisfaction |
| `interaction_type` | Polarity-based interaction classification |

The `ContactMapReport.html` file serves as a central navigation hub, providing organized links to all generated visualizations and data files, with entries grouped by cluster or individual model.

Sources: [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py#L516-L600), [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py#L975-L1070), [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py#L216-L290)

## Integration with HADDOCK3 Workflows

The contactmap module is designed to integrate flexibly within HADDOCK3 workflows. It can be positioned after any module that generates `PDBFile` objects, including docking, refinement, and scoring steps. The module accepts both clustered and unclustered inputs, automatically detecting the input structure type and applying appropriate analysis strategies.

When models contain clustering information (via `cluster_id` and `cluster_rank` attributes), the module performs cluster-based analysis by default. Unclustered models are handled according to the `topX` parameter, which selects a subset of top-scoring models for individual analysis. This dual-mode approach ensures comprehensive contact analysis regardless of upstream processing.

The module does not modify input models; instead, it forwards them unchanged to the next workflow step. This pass-through design allows contact map analysis to serve as an inspection point without affecting downstream calculations.

Sources: [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/__init__.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/__init__.py#L58-L124), [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py#L597-L627)

## Advanced Usage Patterns

### Custom Threshold Tuning

Adjust contact thresholds based on your system's characteristics. For small, rigid interfaces, tighter thresholds (e.g., `shortest_dist_threshold=3.5`) can reduce false positives. For flexible or transient interactions, looser thresholds (e.g., `shortest_dist_threshold=5.5`) capture weaker but potentially important contacts.

### Multi-Stage Analysis

Run contactmap at multiple workflow stages to track interaction evolution. Early stage (e.g., after rigid-body docking) reveals sampling diversity, while later stages (e.g., after refinement) show convergence to stable interfaces. Comparing these analyses identifies which contacts persist through refinement—indicating likely biological relevance.

### Offline Mode

For environments without internet access, use the `offline=True` parameter when calling `tsv_to_heatmap` or `tsv_to_chordchart`. This embeds Plotly JavaScript libraries directly in the HTML files, enabling full interactivity without external dependencies.

Sources: [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/defaults.yaml](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/defaults.yaml#L1-L121), [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py#L1071-L1195)

## Troubleshooting and Common Issues

**Missing Cα Atoms**: The module defaults to using Cα atoms for residue representation. If structures contain non-standard residues or missing Cα atoms, consider lowering `ca_ca_dist_threshold` or relying on `shortest-dist` metrics which use all heavy atoms.

**Large Complex Memory Usage**: For very large complexes (>1000 residues), the all-vs-all distance matrix can consume significant memory. Consider analyzing chains individually or using cluster-based analysis to reduce computational load.

**Visual Clutter in Chord Charts**: Dense interfaces can produce visually crowded chord charts. Use the `filter_intermolecular_contacts` parameter to focus on the strongest contacts, or adjust `shortest_dist_threshold` to include only high-confidence interactions.

**HTML Display Issues**: Ensure your browser supports HTML5 and JavaScript for interactive Plotly visualizations. For static environments, export plots to static image formats using Plotly's `write_image` functionality.

Sources: [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py#L840-L892), [src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py](src/haddock/modules/analysis/contactmap/contmap.py#L2253-L2378)

- [Alanine Scanning for Interface Analysis](24-alanine-scanning-for-interface-analysis) - Systematic evaluation of interface residue importance
- [Result Analysis and Interpretation](25-result-analysis-and-interpretation) - Broader context for interpreting docking results
